--- title: "Data" subtitle: "Where the shade and heat maps come from, and who we follow home." jupyter: python3 --- ## Sources All inputs are public data. | Layer | Source | Used for | | --- | --- | --- | | Airborne LiDAR, March 2022 | City of Philadelphia, via NOAA Digital Coast and PASDA | ground, building and tree heights at 1 m | | Building footprints | City of Philadelphia (OpenDataPhilly) | building outlines | | Land cover 2018 | PASDA | tree canopy | | Canopy height (CHMv2) | Meta / WRI, CC BY 4.0 | trees just outside the city | | Pedestrian network | DVRPC | sidewalks and crosswalks | | OpenStreetMap | OSM contributors, ODbL (Overpass API; Geofabrik extract when Overpass was down) | bridges, covered walkways, campus footways | | Transit | SEPTA, fall 2026 timetable (release v202609271) | rapid-transit stations and frequent bus stops | | Hourly weather | ERA5 reanalysis (ECMWF), via the Open-Meteo archive | air temperature, humidity, wind and sunshine for the heat model | | Heat model | SOLWEIG 2022a, GPU version (solweig-gpu 2.0.0) | mean radiant temperature and UTCI at 1 m | | Properties | City of Philadelphia (OPA) | residential parcels, where walks end | | Land surface temperature | USGS Landsat 8 (July 17, 2024) | the summer heat map on the Story page (Landsat surface temperature, as used for Philadelphia by Li, Chakraborty & Wang 2023, *Urban Climate*) | | Air temperature | NOAA ACIS, Philadelphia International Airport | summer heat figures on the Story page | ## The shade map ::: {.stat-row}
7,237 km
sidewalks and crossings
3.6 M
points checked for shade, every 2 m

height model of buildings and trees
::: Building and tree heights come from the 2022 LiDAR survey, flown before the leaves came out. Building heights agree closely with the city's own records (median absolute difference 0.5 m over 541,222 buildings); bridges and elevated rail lines are included, so they cast shadows too. Trees cover 17% of the city in the model (the median tree is 15 m tall). Covered walkways and passages through buildings (4.2 km) are always in shade. ::: {#4d47a23c .cell .figure-light execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ![University City in the height model: buildings (blue and pink), bridges and other structures (orange) and trees (green).](data_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.jpeg){} ::: ::: ## The heat model Shade says where the sun is blocked; it does not say how hot a sidewalk feels. For that, the same 1 m heights go into SOLWEIG, a model of the radiation a standing person receives from the sun, the sky, walls and the ground, which it turns into the **mean radiant temperature** and, with air temperature, humidity and wind, into the **UTCI** (Universal Thermal Climate Index), a temperature in °C that describes how the weather feels to the body. UTCI above 38 °C is *very strong* heat stress, above 46 °C *extreme*. The model needs real weather, so the study uses two real hot, sunny days of summer 2025 rather than a calendar date: **June 24**, three days after the solstice, during a heat wave, and **July 29**, the nearest hot, sunny day to August 1 (August 1, 2025 itself was cool and overcast). Shadows are computed for the same days and moments, so shade and heat describe the same sidewalks at the same time. | Day | Air temperature, 15:00 | Humidity, 15:00 | Wind, 15:00 | Peak solar radiation | Daily maximum | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | June 24, 2025 | 38.5 °C | 32% | 2.8 m/s | 936 W/m² | 38.8 °C | | July 29, 2025 | 36.1 °C | 43% | 1.8 m/s | 914 W/m² | 36.1 °C | Weather from ERA5 for one 0.25° cell over the city (40.0° N, 75.25° W), used for every sidewalk: the heat map varies with sun, shade, walls and ground, not with air temperature or wind, which are the same everywhere. The model ran in 400 one-kilometre tiles per day on a rented GPU and gives a UTCI value at every one of the 3.6 million sidewalk points, every hour. ## Whose walks Each walk starts at a stop: any rapid-transit station (Regional Rail, L (Market-Frankford), B (Broad Street) or the T trolley tunnel) or a bus stop with at least 6 buses an hour in one direction between 15:00 and 19:00. Every home within 1.2 km walking distance of such a stop is one walk, 431,114 in all. The other 91,659 homes (17.5%), mostly in the Northeast and Roxborough, have no frequent stop that close. ::: {#f1deb721 .cell .figure-light execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ![Homes without a frequent stop within 1.2 km (red).](data_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.jpeg){width=640} ::: ::: ## University City For University City we mapped the entrances and indoor passages of 41 buildings (4.4 km of passages); 10 of them can be entered without a Penn ID. Campus footpaths from OpenStreetMap are added to the sidewalk network there. ## Known gaps - Outside University City, campus and park paths are missing, so cooler options inside campuses and parks are understated. - Shadows assume clear skies on two summer days; trees are mapped from leaf-off LiDAR and 2018 land cover, buildings from 2022. - The heat model uses one weather cell for the whole city: air temperature and wind do not vary between neighbourhoods, so the UTCI map shows the effect of sun, shade and surfaces only. Trees let a fixed 3% of the sun through, and grass, water and paving are from the 2018 land cover. - Missing or misplaced footprints, newer buildings and temporary objects (parked trains, scaffolding) affect shade locally. - The timetable is one weekday in fall 2026; summer service may differ.
